content.title: 2 Introduction
content.narrative_summary: The guideline aims to guide health professionals in managing heart failure (HF) using the best available evidence. It updates the 2016 ESC format to address each HF phenotype separately, presents therapy recommendations by class and evidence level, suggests diagnostic tests for all HF patients, focuses on diagnosis and treatment rather than prevention, and represents a consensus of the Task Force and ESC CPG Committee.

recommendation_tables.title: New recommendations

rows.recommendation: Right heart catheterization should be considered in patients where HF is thought to be due to constrictive pericarditis, restrictive cardiomyopathy, congenital heart disease, and high output states.
Right heart catheterization may be considered in selected patients with HFpEF to confirm the diagnosis.
Dapagliflozin or empagliflozin are recommended for patients with HFrEF to reduce the risk of HF hospitalization and death.

Vericiguat may be considered in patients in NYHA class II–IV who have had worsening HF despite treatment with an ACE-I (or ARNI), a beta-blocker and an MRA to reduce the risk of CV mortality or HF hospitalization.
An ACE-I may be considered for patients with HFmrEF to reduce the risk of HF hospitalization and death.
An ARB may be considered for patients with HFmrEF to reduce the risk of HF hospitalization and death.
A beta-blocker may be considered for patients with HFmrEF to reduce the risk of HF hospitalization and death.
An MRA may be considered for patients with HFmrEF to reduce the risk of HF hospitalization and death.
Sacubitril/valsartan may be considered for patients with HFmrEF to reduce the risk of HF hospitalization and death.
Screening for, and treatment of, aetiologies, and CV and non-CV comorbidities are recommended in patients with HFpEF (see relevant sections of this document).
Self-management strategies are recommended to reduce the risk of HF hospitalization and mortality.
Either home-based and/or clinic-based programmes improve outcomes and are recommended to reduce the risk of HF hospitalization and mortality.
Influenza and pneumococcal vaccinations should be considered in order to prevent HF hospitalizations.
A supervised, exercise-based, cardiac rehabilitation programme should be considered in patients with more severe disease, frailty, or with comorbidities.
Non-invasive HTM may be considered for patients with HF in order to reduce the risk of recurrent CV and HF hospitalizations and CV death.
Patients being considered for long-term MCS must have good compliance, appropriate capacity for device handling and psychosocial support.

content.narrative_summary: This page provides guideline recommendations for the management of heart failure, including advanced therapies such as heart transplantation and inotropes, as well as specific recommendations for patients after hospitalization and those with comorbid conditions: atrial fibrillation, coronary artery disease (CCS), valvular heart disease, diabetes, iron deficiency, cancer, and amyloidosis.

rows.recommendation: Heart transplantation is recommended for patients with advanced HF, refractory to medical/device therapy and who do not have absolute contraindications.
Continuous inotropes and/or vasopressors may be considered in patients with low cardiac output and evidence of organ hypoperfusion as bridge to MCS or heart transplantation.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for management of patients after HF hospitalization

rows.recommendation: It is recommended that patients hospitalized for HF be carefully evaluated to exclude persistent signs of congestion before discharge and to optimize oral treatment.
It is recommended that evidence-based oral medical treatment be administered before discharge.
An early follow-up visit is recommended at 1–2 weeks after discharge to assess signs of congestion, drug tolerance, and start and/or uptitrate evidence-based therapy.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for management of patients with HF and atrial fibrillation

rows.recommendation: Long-term treatment with an oral anticoagulant should be considered for stroke prevention in AF patients with a CHA2DS2-VASc score of 1 in men or 2 in women.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for management of patients with HF and CCS

rows.recommendation: CABG should be considered as the first-choice revascularization strategy, in patients suitable for surgery, especially if they have diabetes and for those with multivessel disease.
In LVAD candidates needing coronary revascularization, CABG should be avoided, if possible.

Coronary revascularization may be considered to improve outcomes in patients with HFrEF, CCS, and coronary anatomy suitable for revascularization, after careful evaluation of the individual risk to benefit ratio, including coronary anatomy (i.e. proximal stenosis >90% of large vessels, stenosis of left main or proximal LAD), comorbidities, life expectancy, and patient’s perspectives.
PCI may be considered as alternative to CABG, based on Heart Team evaluation, considering coronary anatomy, comorbidities, and surgical risk.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for management of patients with HF and valvular heart disease

rows.recommendation: Aortic valve intervention, TAVI or SAVR is recommended in patients with HF and severe high-gradient aortic stenosis to reduce mortality and improve symptoms.

It is recommended that the choice between TAVI and SAVR be made by the Heart Team, according to individual patient preference and features including age, surgical risk, clinical, anatomical and procedural aspects, weighing the risks and benefits of each approach.

Percutaneous edge-to-edge mitral valve repair should be considered in carefully selected patients with secondary mitral regurgitation, not eligible for surgery and not needing coronary revascularization, who are symptomatic despite OMT and who fulfil criteria to achieve a reduction in HF hospitalizations.

Percutaneous edge-to-edge mitral valve repair may be considered to improve symptoms in carefully selected patients with secondary mitral regurgitation, not eligible for surgery and not needing coronary revascularization, who are highly symptomatic despite OMT and who do not fulfil criteria for reducing HF hospitalization.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for management of patients with HF and diabetes

rows.recommendation: SGLT2 inhibitors (canagliflozin, dapagliflozin, empagliflozin, ertugliflozin, sotagliflozin) are recommended in patients with T2DM at risk of CV events to reduce hospitalizations for HF, major CV events, end-stage renal dysfunction, and CV death.
SGLT2 inhibitors (dapagliflozin, empagliflozin, and sotagliflozin) are recommended in patients with T2DM and HFrEF to reduce hospitalizations for HF and CV death.
The DPP-4 inhibitor saxagliptin is not recommended in patients with HF.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for management of patients with HF and iron deficiency

rows.recommendation: It is recommended that all patients with HF are periodically screened for anaemia and iron deficiency with a full blood count, serum ferritin concentration, and TSAT.

Intravenous iron supplementation with ferric carboxymaltose should be considered in symptomatic HF patients recently hospitalized for HF and with LVEF ≤50% and iron deficiency, defined as serum ferritin <100 ng/mL or serum ferritin 100–299 ng/mL with TSAT <20%, to reduce the risk of HF hospitalization.
Treatment of anaemia in HF with erythropoietin stimulating agents is not recommended in the absence of other indications for this therapy.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for management of patients with HF and cancer

rows.recommendation: It is recommended that cancer patients at increased risk for cardiotoxicity, defined by a history or risk factors of CV disease, previous cardiotoxicity or exposure to cardiotoxic agents, undergo CV evaluation before scheduled anticancer therapy, preferably by a cardiologist with experience/interest in Cardio-Oncology.

Treatment with an ACE-I and a beta-blocker (preferably carvedilol) should be considered in cancer patients developing LV systolic dysfunction, defined as a 10% or more decrease in LVEF and to a value lower than 50%, during anthracycline chemotherapy.
A baseline CV risk assessment should be considered in all cancer patients scheduled to receive a cancer treatment with the potential to cause HF.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for treatment of patients with HF and amyloidosis

rows.recommendation: Tafamidis is recommended in patients with genetic testing proven hATTR-CA and NYHA class I or II symptoms to reduce symptoms, CV hospitalization and mortality.
Tafamidis is recommended in patients with wtATTR-CA and NYHA class I or II symptoms to reduce symptoms, CV hospitalization and mortality.

section_headings: 3.2.1 Heart failure with preserved, mildly reduced, and reduced ejection fraction
content.narrative_summary: Section 3.1 defines heart failure (HF) as a clinical syndrome of cardinal symptoms (e.g., breathlessness, ankle swelling, fatigue) and signs (e.g., elevated jugular venous pressure, pulmonary crackles, peripheral oedema) due to structural and/or functional cardiac abnormalities leading to elevated intracardiac pressures or inadequate output. Identification of the underlying aetiology is mandatory to guide treatment, with most cases due to systolic and/or diastolic myocardial dysfunction. Section 3.2.1 discusses the classification of HF by left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF): reduced LVEF ≤40% (HFrEF), mildly reduced 41–49% (HFmrEF), and notes that patients with LVEF in the 40–50% range may benefit similarly to those with lower LVEF.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for management of patients with HF and AF

rows.recommendation: DOACs are recommended in preference to VKAs in patients with HF, except in those with moderate or severe mitral stenosis or mechanical prosthetic heart valves.

For patients with HF and non-valvular AF eligible for anticoagulation based on a CHA2DS2-VASc score, NOACs rather than warfarin should be considered for anticoagulation as NOACs are associated with a lower risk of stroke, intracranial haemorrhage, and mortality, which outweigh the increased risk of gastrointestinal haemorrhage.
Beta-blockers should be considered for short- and long-term rate control in patients with HF and AF.
For patients in NYHA class I–III, a beta-blocker, usually given orally, is safe and therefore is recommended as first-line treatment to control ventricular rate, provided the patient is euvolaemic.

In cases of a clear association between paroxysmal or persistent AF and worsening of HF symptoms, which persist despite medical therapy, catheter ablation should be considered for the prevention of AF.

AV node catheter ablation may be considered to control heart rate and relieve symptoms in patients unresponsive or intolerant to intensive pharmacological rate and rhythm control therapy, accepting that these patients will become pacemaker-dependent.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for management of patients with HF and CCS

rows.recommendation: Coronary revascularization should be considered to relieve persistent symptoms of angina (or an angina-equivalent) in patients with HFrEF, CCS, and coronary anatomy suitable for revascularization, despite OMT including anti-anginal drugs.
Myocardial revascularization is recommended when angina persists despite treatment with anti-anginal drugs.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for management of patients with HF and diabetes

rows.recommendation: SGLT2 inhibitors (canagliflozin, dapagliflozin, empagliflozin, ertugliflozin, sotagliflozin) are recommended in patients with T2DM at risk of CV events to reduce hospitalizations for HF, major CV events, end-stage renal dysfunction, and CV death.
Empagliflozin should be considered in patients with T2DM in order to prevent or delay the onset of HF and prolong life.

section_headings: 4.1 Key steps in the diagnosis of chronic heart failure
content.narrative_summary: Table 4 presents the New York Heart Association functional classification based on symptoms and physical activity. Approximately 50% of patients with heart failure (HF) have reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) and 50% have preserved or mid-range EF, with some registries reporting 60% HFrEF, 24% HFmrEF, and 16% HFpEF. Aetiology varies by geography, with coronary artery disease and hypertension as predominant factors in Western populations. Prognosis has improved since early treatment trials but remains poor, especially in HFrEF, with 1- and 5-year mortality rates of 20% and 53%, respectively. Transition between HF phenotypes over time is common, and those progressing to HFrEF have worse outcomes. Section 4 introduces chronic HF, outlining key diagnostic steps including symptoms, signs, and recommended tests such as ECG.

figures_tables_algorithms.title: New York Heart Association functional classification based on severity of symptoms and physical activity
figures_tables_algorithms.summary:
Class I: No limitation of physical activity. Ordinary physical activity does not cause undue breathlessness, fatigue, or palpitations.
Class II: Slight limitation of physical activity. Comfortable at rest, but ordinary physical activity results in undue breathlessness, fatigue, or palpitations.
Class III: Marked limitation of physical activity. Comfortable at rest, but less than ordinary activity results undue breathlessness, fatigue, or palpitations.
Class IV: Unable to carry on any physical activity without discomfort. Symptoms at rest can be present. If any physical activity is undertaken, discomfort is increased.

content.narrative_summary: Figure 1 presents a diagnostic flowchart for suspected heart failure, starting with risk factors, symptoms/signs, and ECG. It guides using natriuretic peptide levels (NT-proBNP ≥125 pg/mL or BNP ≥35 pg/mL) or direct echocardiography if strongly suspected. Abnormal echocardiographic findings confirm heart failure and prompt LVEF-based phenotyping (HFrEF ≤40%, HFmrEF 41–49%, HFpEF ≥50%), followed by aetiology determination and treatment. Normal findings deem heart failure unlikely and suggest considering other diagnoses.

content.narrative_summary: Describes various imaging modalities for assessment of inducible ischaemia and myocardial characterization in heart failure, including exercise or pharmacological stress echocardiography, CMR with late gadolinium enhancement and T1 mapping, computed tomography coronary angiography, single-photon emission CT (SPECT), and technetium-labelled bisphosphonate scintigraphy for cardiac transthyretin amyloid.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for specialized diagnostic tests for selected patients with chronic heart failure to detect reversible/treatable causes of heart failure

rows.recommendation: CMR is recommended for the assessment of myocardial structure and function in those with poor echocardiogram acoustic windows.

CMR is recommended for the characterization of myocardial tissue in suspected infiltrative disease, Fabry disease, inflammatory disease (myocarditis), LV non-compaction, amyloid, sarcoidosis, iron overload/haemochromatosis.
CMR with LGE should be considered in DCM to distinguish between ischaemic and non-ischaemic myocardial damage.
Invasive coronary angiography is recommended in patients with angina despite pharmacological therapy or symptomatic ventricular arrhythmias.
Invasive coronary angiography may be considered in patients with HFrEF with an intermediate to high pre-test probability of CAD and the presence of ischaemia in non-invasive stress tests.
CTCA should be considered in patients with a low to intermediate pre-test probability of CAD or those with equivocal non-invasive stress tests in order to rule out coronary artery stenosis.

Non-invasive stress imaging (CMR, stress echocardiography, SPECT, PET) may be considered for the assessment of myocardial ischaemia and viability in patients with CAD who are considered suitable for coronary revascularization.

content.narrative_summary: Management can be subdivided into three stages (pre-hospital, in-hospital, and pre-discharge) with different goals. In the pre-hospital setting, patients benefit from non-invasive monitoring (pulse oximetry, blood pressure, heart rate, respiratory rate, continuous ECG) initiated within minutes of contact and in the ambulance if possible. Oxygen therapy is given based on clinical judgment or if saturation is <90%; in respiratory distress (rate >25 breaths/min, saturation <90%), non-invasive ventilation should be initiated. The effect of pre-hospital therapeutic tools on clinical outcomes remains to be proven in randomized trials, and rapid transfer to appropriate medical settings should not be delayed. In-hospital management involves prompt diagnostic workup and initiation of pharmacological and non-pharmacological treatments in parallel, with triage according to hemodynamic instability and severity and disposition decisions based on clinical severity and care settings.

content.narrative_summary: The page continues the discussion of catheter ablation versus medical therapy (MT) in patients with AF and HF, noting improvements in symptoms but inconclusive effects on mortality and hospitalization. It then addresses ventricular arrhythmias in HF, recommending correction of precipitating factors, amiodarone for suppression of arrhythmias, and possible radiofrequency ablation of VPBs. The section on symptomatic bradycardia outlines pacemaker therapy indications in HF, warns of adverse effects of RV pacing on LV function, and suggests CRT or His bundle pacing as preferred approaches. The narrative ends with the introduction of chronic coronary syndromes as a common cause of HF and the recommended diagnostic workup.

rows.recommendation: Long-term treatment with an oral anticoagulant is recommended in all patients with AF, HF, and CHA₂DS₂-VASc score ≥2 in men or ≥3 in women.7
DOACs are recommended in preference to VKAs in patients with HF, except in those with moderate or severe mitral stenosis or mechanical prosthetic heart valves.528,558
Long-term treatment with an oral anticoagulant should be considered for stroke prevention in AF patients with a CHA₂DS₂-VASc score of 1 in men or 2 in women.7,559
Beta-blockers should be considered for short-and long-term rate control in patients with HF and AF.535
Digoxin should be considered when the ventricular rate remains high, despite beta-blockers, or when beta-blockers are contraindicated or not tolerated.536
Urgent ECV is recommended in the setting of acute worsening of HF in patients presenting with rapid ventricular rates and haemodynamic instability.
Cardioversion may be considered in patients in whom there is an association between AF and worsening of HF symptoms despite optimal medical treatment.7,541

In cases of a clear association between paroxysmal or persistent AF and worsening of HF symptoms, which persist despite MT, catheter ablation should be considered for the prevention or treatment of AF.552–554,557

content.narrative_summary: This section describes medical therapy in patients with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) and chronic coronary syndrome (CCS). Beta-blockers are recommended as first-line therapy for prognostic benefit, with ivabradine as an alternative or additional anti-anginal agent in patients in sinus rhythm with heart rate ≥70 bpm. Other anti-anginal drugs (amlodipine, felodipine, nicorandil, ranolazine, trimetazidine, nitrates) may be used for symptom relief, although evidence on outcomes is neutral or lacking; trimetazidine may improve left ventricular function and exercise capacity. Short-acting nitrates should be used cautiously due to hypotension; diltiazem and verapamil are contraindicated in HFrEF. In HFpEF, similar agents may relieve angina without proven benefit on heart failure endpoints. Low-dose rivaroxaban did not reduce death, MI, or stroke in HFrEF with CCS (COMMANDER-HF) but showed ischaemic event reduction in HF patients in a COMPASS subgroup, suggesting possible use in patients with CAD or peripheral artery disease.

PCI may be considered as an alternative to CABG, based on Heart Team evaluation, considering coronary anatomy, comorbidities, and surgical risk.

content.title: Figure 16 Management of patients with severe low-flow low-gradient aortic stenosis and heart failure
content.narrative_summary: This page presents a complete flowchart algorithm for the management of patients with heart failure and suspected severe low-flow low-gradient aortic stenosis (AS). Initial evaluation is based on left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF <50 %) with dobutamine echocardiography to assess flow reserve. Depending on flow reserve and calcium score by CT, patients are directed to medical therapy optimization (Class I), Heart Team review (Class I), surgical aortic valve replacement (SAVR; Class I or IIa), transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI; Class I or IIa), or follow-up. Footnotes define diagnostic criteria (valve area ≤1 cm2, mean gradient <40 mmHg, stroke volume index ≤35 mL/m2), flow reserve (% increase in stroke volume index ≥20 %), calcium score thresholds (≥3000 Agatston units in men, ≥1600 in women for very likely AS; lower thresholds to exclude AS), and age- and risk-based recommendations for SAVR vs. TAVI. Additional notes recommend procedures in centres with both interventional cardiology and cardiac surgery, and consider balloon aortic valvuloplasty as a bridge in advanced heart failure.

content.narrative_summary: Secondary mitral regurgitation (SMR) is a dynamic condition primarily affecting the left ventricle, often due to annular enlargement from LA dilation. content.narrative_summary: This page discusses outcomes of various diabetes treatments in patients with heart failure. SGLT2 inhibitors (canagliflozin, dapagliflozin, empagliflozin, ertugliflozin, sotagliflozin) reduce cardiovascular and heart failure events, hospitalizations, and renal outcomes, and are recommended for patients with type 2 diabetes at risk of CV events or with HFrEF. Insulin and sulfonylureas may worsen outcomes in HF and require close monitoring if used, while thiazolidinediones are contraindicated due to fluid retention and increased HF hospitalizations. Metformin is generally safe except in severe renal or hepatic impairment. DPP-4 inhibitors showed neutral or harmful effects on HF outcomes.

section_headings: 13.7 Electrolyte disorders: hypokalaemia, hyperkalaemia, hyponatraemia, hypochloraemia
content.narrative_summary: This section discusses the frequency, definitions, classification, and management of electrolyte disturbances in heart failure. Hypokalaemia (serum K+ <3.5 mmol/L) often results from loop and thiazide diuretics and may require RAAS inhibitors, potassium-sparing diuretics, oral or intravenous potassium supplementation. Hyperkalaemia (serum K+ >5 mmol/L) is linked to RAAS inhibitors, CKD, and reduced excretion; treatment options include calcium carbonate, sodium bicarbonate, insulin, beta-adrenoceptor agonists, loop diuretics, and potassium binders (e.g., sodium polystyrene sulfonate, SZC, patiromer). Hyponatraemia (serum Na+ <136 mmol/L) reflects neurohormonal activation, may require hypertonic saline for severe cases, and is a marker of poor outcomes in acute and chronic HF.

content.narrative_summary: Section 13.10 discusses hyperuricaemia in chronic heart failure (CHF), noting its prevalence and association with diuretic therapy, exercise capacity, and prognosis. Both febuxostat and allopurinol lower uric acid levels, but allopurinol is preferred as first-line urate-lowering therapy. Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs can worsen HF, so colchicine is preferred for acute gout with caution in renal dysfunction. High-dose anti-tumour necrosis factor α agents may worsen HF. Section 13.11 addresses erectile dysfunction in HF patients, its multifactorial etiology, prevalence, and assessment. Some cardiovascular drugs (e.g., diuretics, beta-blockers) are implicated; phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors are generally safe in compensated HF but contraindicated with nitrates or within specified timeframes of sildenafil, vardenafil, or tadalafil. Section 13.12 covers depression in HF, affecting about 20% of patients, with higher rates in women and association with worse prognosis. Screening with validated questionnaires is recommended; psychosocial interventions improve symptoms but not prognosis. Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors may help but trials show mixed results; tricyclics should be avoided. Section 13.13 describes HF in cancer patients due to cardiotoxic therapies or cancer itself, recommending integrated cardio-oncology assessment using HFA-ICOS baseline risk tools. History of HF or cardiomyopathy and LVEF <50% identify high-risk patients.

content.narrative_summary: The narrative emphasizes monitoring left ventricular (LV) systolic function during potentially cardiotoxic cancer therapy through echocardiography, with baseline measurement of natriuretic peptides (NPs) or troponin. section_headings: 14.1.2 New heart failure presenting during pregnancy
content.narrative_summary: Infections can worsen heart failure (HF) symptoms and precipitate acute HF; severe sepsis and pneumonia may cause myocardial injury and cardiac dysfunction with higher risk in patients with a history of HF. The COVID-19 pandemic is a major cause of morbidity and HF decompensation. Influenza, pneumococcal, and COVID-19 vaccinations are associated with reduced all-cause mortality and should be considered in patients with HF. Women with pre-existing HF face increased risk of pregnancy-related cardiovascular complications; those at moderate or high risk (mWHO class III–IV) should be referred to a multidisciplinary Pregnancy Heart Team. Pre-pregnancy management includes stopping contraindicated HF medications (ACE-Is, ARBs, ARNIs, MRAs, ivabradine, SGLT2 inhibitors), continuing beta-blockers, and initiating hydralazine, oral nitrates, or methyldopa if needed. Anticoagulation with LMWH in the first and third trimesters (and VKAs or LMWH in the second trimester) is recommended for HF with atrial fibrillation; DOACs should be avoided. Assessment at new pregnancy (symptoms, examination, BP, SaO₂, ECG, echocardiography) and multidisciplinary planning of delivery around 35 weeks, with periodic reassessment based on mWHO class, is advised.

Treatment with an ACE‐I and a beta‐blocker (preferably carvedilol) should be considered in cancer patients developing LV systolic dysfunction, defined as a 10% or more decrease in LVEF and to a value lower than 50%, during anthracycline chemotherapy.
A baseline CV risk assessment should be considered in all cancer patients scheduled to receive a cancer treatment with the potential to cause heart failure.

content.title: Table 28. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy: specific aspects of diagnosis and treatment
content.narrative_summary: This table summarizes key diagnostic criteria and management strategies for hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM), including morphologic definition, differential diagnoses, recommendations for genetic counselling and testing (with a minimal gene panel), indications for endomyocardial biopsy, and therapeutic options stratified by presence of LV outflow tract obstruction, ICD indications, and specific diseases such as Fabry and amyloidosis.

recommendation_tables.title: Table 28. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy: specific aspects of diagnosis and treatment

rows.recommendation: Wall thickness >14 mm in one or more LV myocardial segments not sufficiently explained solely by abnormal loading conditions. LVOTO ≥30 mmHg at rest or exercise, asymmetric hypertrophy, or increased LGE in a patchy mid-wall pattern in the most hypertrophied segment, further suggest the presence of HCM. It can be considered familial when two or more first- or second-degree relatives with HCM or a first-degree relative with autopsy proven HCM and sudden death at <50 years of age are detected.

It might be difficult with physiological hypertrophy induced by intense athletic training, severe hypertension or aortic stenosis and with isolated septal hypertrophy. Consider a genetic HCM if the degree of LV hypertrophy is disproportionate with respect to the acquired trigger. Consider amyloidosis as a cause when increased thickness of the interatrial septum, AV valve and/or RV free wall are detected (see section 14.6).

Indication. Must be offered to all patients with a diagnosis of HCM to identify a possible underlying genetic cause and to all first-degree adult relatives of patients with HCM and a definite disease-causing mutation, regardless of their phenotype, in order to identify genetically affected individuals at a preclinical phase. Clinical evaluation, ECG and echocardiography must be performed in first-degree relatives who have the same definite disease-causing mutation as the index patient. When no definite genetic mutation is identified in the index patient or genetic testing is not performed, clinical evaluation with ECG and echocardiography should be considered in first-degree adult relatives and repeated every 2–5 years or less if non-diagnostic abnormalities are present.

content.narrative_summary: Section 14.4 describes atrial disease as subclinical structural, electrophysiological, and functional atrial changes with potential clinical consequences, interrelated with HF and AF. Diagnosis relies on multimodality imaging (echocardiography, CT, CMR) and biomarkers (high-sensitivity troponins, natriuretic peptides), though a comprehensive characterization remains lacking. Management is emerging, targeting prevention of AF, thromboembolism, and HFpEF. Section 14.5 covers myocarditis, estimated at 1.5 million cases per year, contributing to HF in 0.5–4% of patients; EMB-proven inflammation occurs in 9–30% of DCM cases. Clinical presentation ranges from mild symptoms to cardiogenic shock; diagnosis uses biopsy and CMR. Treatment involves hospitalization for at least 48 hours, standard HF therapy, and immunosuppression in selected cases after excluding active viral infection; immunomodulatory trials are ongoing. Section 14.6 notes amyloid cardiomyopathy (AL and ATTR types) as an underdiagnosed cause of HF; ATTR comprises wild-type (>90%) and variant (<10%) forms, with an estimated 6–16% prevalence of CA among HF patients.

CMR is recommended for the characterization of myocardial tissue in suspected infiltrative disease, Fabry disease, inflammatory disease (myocarditis), LV non-compaction, amyloid, sarcoidosis, iron overload/haemochromatosis.
Invasive coronary angiography is recommended in patients with angina despite pharmacological therapy or symptomatic ventricular arrhythmias.
Cardiopulmonary exercise testing is recommended as a part of the evaluation for heart transplantation and/or MCS.

ACE-I is recommended for patients with HFrEF to reduce the risk of HF hospitalization and death.
Beta-blocker is recommended for patients with stable HFrEF to reduce the risk of HF hospitalization and death.
MRA is recommended for patients with HFrEF to reduce the risk of HF hospitalization and death.
Dapagliflozin or empagliflozin are recommended for patients with HFrEF to reduce the risk of HF hospitalization and death.
Sacubitril/valsartan is recommended as a replacement for an ACE-I in patients with HFrEF to reduce the risk of HF hospitalization and death.
Diuretics are recommended in patients with HFrEF with signs and/or symptoms of congestion to alleviate HF symptoms, improve exercise capacity and reduce HF hospitalizations.
An ARBc is recommended to reduce the risk of HF hospitalization and CV death in symptomatic patients unable to tolerate an ACE-I or ARNI (patients should also receive a beta-blocker and an MRA).
The addition of an ARB (or renin inhibitor) to the combination of an ACE-I and an MRA is not recommended in patients with HF, because of the increased risk of renal dysfunction and hyperkalaemia.

An ICD is recommended to reduce the risk of sudden death and all-cause mortality in patients who have recovered from a ventricular arrhythmia causing haemodynamic instability, and who are expected to survive for >1 year with good functional status, in the absence of reversible causes or unless the ventricular arrhythmia has occurred <48 h after a MI.

An ICD is recommended to reduce the risk of sudden death and all-cause mortality in patients with symptomatic HF (NYHA class II–III) of an ischaemic aetiology (unless they have had an MI in the prior 40 days—see below), and an LVEF ≤35% despite ≥3 months of OMT, provided they are expected to survive substantially longer than 1 year with good functional status.
ICD implantation is not recommended within 40 days of an MI as implantation at this time does not improve prognosis.
ICD therapy is not recommended in patients in NYHA class IV with severe symptoms refractory to pharmacological therapy unless they are candidates for CRT, a VAD, or cardiac transplantation.

CRT is recommended for symptomatic patients with HF in SR with a QRS duration ≥150 ms and LBBB QRS morphology and with LVEF ≤35% despite OMT in order to improve symptoms and reduce morbidity and mortality.

CRT rather than RV pacing is recommended for patients with HFrEF regardless of NYHA class or QRS width who have an indication for ventricular pacing for high degree AV block in order to reduce morbidity. This includes patients with AF.
CRT is not recommended in patients with a QRS duration <130 ms who do not have an indication for pacing due to high-degree AV block.
Diuretics are recommended in patients with congestion and HFmrEF in order to alleviate symptoms and signs.

Counselling against sedentary habit, obesity, cigarette smoking, and alcohol abuse is recommended to prevent or delay the onset of HF.
It is recommended that HF patients are enrolled in a multidisciplinary HF management programme to reduce the risk of HF hospitalization and mortality.
Self-management strategies are recommended to reduce the risk of HF hospitalization and mortality.
Either home-based and/or clinic-based programmes improve outcomes and are recommended to reduce the risk of HF hospitalization and mortality.

Intubation is recommended for progressive respiratory failure persisting in spite of oxygen administration or non-invasive ventilation.
Intravenous loop diuretics are recommended for all patients with AHF admitted with signs/symptoms of fluid overload to improve symptoms.

Inotropic agents are not recommended routinely, due to safety concerns, unless the patient has symptomatic hypotension and evidence of hypoperfusion.
Routine use of opiates is not recommended, unless in selected patients with severe/intractable pain or anxiety.
IABP is not routinely recommended in post-MI cardiogenic shock.

It is recommended that evidence-based oral medical treatment be administered before discharge.
